Title: Global Case Studies and Practical Framework for AIGC in Primary and Secondary Classrooms

Executive Summary
Generative AI (AIGC) has rapidly entered K-12 classrooms worldwide, prompting both opportunities and challenges for teaching and learning. Evidence from Finland, South Korea, Singapore, and the United States shows that AIGC can enhance creativity, collaboration, and feedback practices when integrated thoughtfully. An MIT perspective emphasizes that generative AI is an “arrival” technology that students are already using, requiring proactive frameworks for ethical, pedagogically sound implementation<cite id="9">Generative AI is an “arrival” technology; students are using it on school assignments regardless of school policy, and educators face a spectrum of reactions from optimism to pessimism.</cite>.

Framework for AIGC in K-12 Classrooms
A practical framework for AIGC in K-12 classrooms should include: (1) pedagogical purpose and learning goals; (2) student-centered, scaffolded activities; (3) ethical and critical AI literacy; (4) teacher roles as facilitators and co-learners; and (5) assessment aligned to authentic tasks. This approach is consistent with project-based, creative, and ethics-infused curricula designed for middle schoolers and aligns with international efforts to teach AI literacy and responsible use<cite id="37">Three middle school AI literacy curricula emphasize active learning, embedded ethics, and low barriers to access to empower students to create and critique AI artifacts.</cite><cite id="9">MIT recommends balancing new practices with traditional ones and focusing on personal interactions as teachers adapt to generative AI.</cite>.

Application Categories and Global Case Studies
1. Creative Writing and Language Arts
In South Korea, an elementary English writing program using image-generative AI (Padlet’s “I Can’t Draw”) improved syntactic and lexical complexity and fluency, increased situational interest, and boosted student engagement and motivation. The program, developed with ADDIE and aligned to national curriculum standards, highlights the importance of teacher competence in integrating AI into language instruction<cite id="28">An elementary English writing program using image-generative AI improved syntactic/lexical complexity and fluency, increased situational interest, and enhanced engagement; teacher competence was emphasized.</cite>.

2. Visual Arts and Creative Expression
A Singaporean study of art educators’ reflections on AI art education underscores transformative pedagogies that use AI tools to expand creative possibilities while foregrounding pedagogical intention and critical reflection. This case illustrates how educators can guide students to explore AI-generated art within a meaningful, human-centered curriculum<cite id="36">Art educators in Singapore reflect on AI art education as transformative, emphasizing pedagogical intention and critical reflection in integrating AI into art education.</cite>.

3. Collaborative, Project-Based Learning and Cultural Education
In Finland, primary school classes used ChatGPT-3.5 to personalize learning materials so they could meet varying knowledge levels and skills, with a clear majority of pupils enjoying the AI-modified content. The study across 4th–6th grades in two schools demonstrates that AIGC can support inclusive, motivated learning when used to adapt and personify content<cite id="27">In primary schools, ChatGPT-3.5 was used to personify learning material to different knowledge levels; most pupils enjoyed it, indicating potential for inclusive, motivated learning.</cite>.

4. Coding and Creative Computing
Scratch Copilot, an AI assistant designed for the Scratch visual programming environment, supports ideation, code generation, debugging, and code understanding for middle schoolers. Early evaluations suggest it can boost creative self-efficacy and engagement, offering a pathway to integrate AI-assisted coding into youth computing education<cite id="35">Scratch Copilot provides real-time support for ideation, code generation, and debugging in Scratch; qualitative findings indicate support for creative self-efficacy and engagement.</cite>.

5. Curriculum Design and Teacher Collaboration
A qualitative study of teachers and administrators using MagicSchool AI during a month-long curriculum design workshop shows how AI can mediate collaborative lesson planning. Through embodied co-agency and human-AI feedback loops, educators co-created cross-disciplinary lessons for a virtual special education program, illustrating AI’s potential to support teacher collaboration and design<cite id="2">Teachers and administrators mediated by MagicSchool AI co-designed lessons using human-AI feedback loops and embodied co-agency, culminating in deployable lesson plans.</cite>.

6. Aesthetic and Cultural Education with AI-Generated Media
A case study on teaching traditional Chinese cultural concepts (the Twenty-Four Solar Terms) combined scaffolding instruction with AI-driven diffusion models to generate instructional images and structure learning activities. Students showed deeper understanding of cultural symbolism and increased engagement, with benefits for both classroom and distance learning contexts<cite id="14">A scaffolding framework with an AI-driven diffusion model generated instructional images and improved students’ engagement and comprehension of traditional cultural concepts.</cite>.

Practical Implementation Methods
- Align AIGC use to clear learning goals and scaffold student tasks. For example, in the English writing program, activities were designed with ADDIE and aligned to national standards, ensuring that AI tools supported language development rather than replacing it<cite id="28">Program design followed ADDIE and aligned with national curriculum standards, supporting language development with AI tools.</cite>.
- Foster student-centered, collaborative projects. Finland’s use of ChatGPT-3.5 to personalize content and Finland’s broader project-based approach show how AIGC can be embedded in group tasks to meet diverse needs and increase motivation<cite id="27">AI-modified materials met varying knowledge levels and increased enjoyment among students.</cite>.
- Integrate AI literacy and ethics. Project-based curricula for middle school emphasize teaching students to create and critique AI artifacts while embedding ethical reflection, providing a model for responsible AIGC use in classrooms<cite id="37">Curricula combine hands-on creation with ethical reflection to develop a critical lens on AI.</cite>.
- Support teachers as co-learners and designers. Tools like MagicSchool AI can facilitate curriculum design and teacher collaboration, while teacher competence and professional development are critical for successful integration<cite id="2">AI-mediated curriculum design supported teacher collaboration and co-agency.</cite><cite id="28">Teacher competence was emphasized as critical for integrating AI into language instruction.</cite>.
- Use AIGC to enhance feedback and assessment practices. Natural-language explanations from generative AI can improve educators’ feedback quality and satisfaction compared to minimal highlights, offering an auxiliary support model for grading and formative feedback<cite id="23">Natural-language grading insights significantly improved feedback quality and educator satisfaction compared to important-word highlights.</cite>.

Future Trends
- Increased adoption of AI-assisted creative tools in coding and arts. Early prototypes like Scratch Copilot suggest growing support for youth creative coding, while Singaporean reflections highlight AI’s expanding role in art education<cite id="35">AI-assisted coding in Scratch supports ideation and debugging for middle schoolers.</cite><cite id="36">Transformative AI art education practices are emerging in Singapore.</cite>.
- Ethics and critical AI literacy becoming core competencies. Curricula that pair creation with ethical reflection indicate a shift toward teaching students to engage critically with AI systems and their societal impacts<cite id="37">Embedded ethics and active learning are central to AI literacy curricula.</cite>.
- Personalized, adaptive learning with AIGC. Evidence from Finland shows that AIGC can be used to personify and adapt content to diverse learners, a trend likely to expand as tools and pedagogies mature<cite id="27">AIGC was used to personify learning material to meet different knowledge levels and skills.</cite>.
- Blended and distance learning applications. AI-generated media and scaffolding frameworks can enhance both classroom and online cultural and art education, supporting inclusive access and engagement<cite id="14">AI-driven diffusion models can generate high-quality instructional resources for classroom and distance learning.</cite>.

Recommendations for Educators
- Start with clear learning goals and scaffolded activities. Choose AIGC tools that directly support curricular objectives, such as image generation for writing prompts or code generation for creative computing, and provide structured guidance<cite id="28">Align AI tools with curriculum standards and use structured design to support language development.</cite><cite id="35">AI-assisted coding should be scaffolded to support ideation and debugging for novice learners.</cite>.
- Co-design with colleagues and students. Use AI to facilitate collaborative curriculum design and co-creative tasks, encouraging human-AI feedback loops and shared ownership of learning<cite id="2">Collaborative, AI-mediated curriculum design supports co-agency and inquiry.</cite>.
- Teach AI literacy and ethics. Incorporate lessons on creating, critiquing, and responsibly using AI artifacts, helping students develop a critical lens on technology’s societal role<cite id="37">Embed ethics in AI creation activities to foster critical understanding.</cite>.
- Use AIGC to enhance feedback and assessment. Provide educators with natural-language insights as auxiliary feedback tools to improve feedback quality and efficiency while maintaining academic integrity<cite id="23">Natural-language AI insights improved feedback quality and educator satisfaction.</cite>.
- Monitor and adapt based on student needs and engagement. Finland’s evidence that students enjoy AI-personified content suggests that personalization and motivation are key success factors; continuously assess how AIGC impacts diverse learners<cite id="27">Students’ enjoyment and motivation increased when content was adapted with AIGC.</cite>.
- Invest in teacher professional learning. Teacher competence and confidence are essential for integrating AI tools effectively; provide ongoing support and opportunities to co-design and experiment<cite id="28">Teacher competence was identified as critical for successful AI integration in language instruction.</cite>.

Conclusion
Global case studies demonstrate that AIGC can enrich K-12 classrooms when grounded in clear pedagogy, ethical reflection, and student-centered design. From language writing and creative coding to collaborative curriculum design and cultural education, evidence shows both engagement gains and learning improvements when AIGC is used intentionally. As adoption grows, educators should prioritize frameworks that balance innovation with responsibility, ensuring that AIGC supports higher-order thinking and meaningful learning<cite id="9">MIT calls for balancing new practices with traditional ones and focusing on personal interactions as schools adapt.</cite><cite id="37">Project-based AI curricula emphasize active learning and ethics to empower students.</cite>.
</answer>

Despite the advocacy to leverage Artificial Intelligence (AI) to automate assessment, concerns persist regarding inaccurate AI assessment on student learning and the potential detrimental effects on educators’ assessment practices due to reliance. One alternative is to leverage AI-powered assessment insights as auxiliary information to support educators’ assessment instead of solely entrusting AI for assessment. However, insights published in existing literature typically required excessive cognitive efforts from human graders to interpret and make use of. Generative AI (GenAI) technologies’ capability To produce natural-language assessment explanations could potentially tackle this challenge. To empirically examine the efficacy of such natural-language insights while accounting for concerns in over-reliance on AI, we invited 60 human graders from diverse backgrounds to participate in multiple phases of assessment for secondary students’ short-answer responses. Participants were assigned to one of the three conditions: no AI-powered assessment support; important-word highlights from AI-powered graders as support; and natural-language grading explanations from GenAI-powered graders as support. Mixed-effect regression analyses were adopted to examine the impacts of different AI-powered assessment insights on human assessment practices both in current assessment with AI-powered insights presented and in later assessment without AI-powered insights. Our findings indicate that GenAI-enabled natural-language insights significantly improved educators’ feedback quality compared to educators without AI support (, ). Important-word highlights from traditional AI graders had negligible impact on educators’ feedback quality. ABSTRACT
In November of 2022, a Silicon Valley company launched an invention that could complete students’ homework for them. Available only to subscribers at first, by the spring of 2023 OpenAI’s ChatGPT-3.5 was available to millions of students. As of January 2023, anyone with internet service can access the next generation, GPT-4, using Microsoft’s Bing, for free. ChatGPT and other emerging models like it are a form of generative AI, and its widespread availability poses new challenges and opportunities for schools. The response from educators falls along a spectrum, of enthusiasm and optimism on one side, and fatigue, bitterness, and pessimism on the other, and commonly, a mix of positive and negative attitudes. The optimists, the pessimists, and the ambivalent all agree that the sudden, widespread availability of generative AI has been a jolt that has left them scrambling to adapt for the past year.
I saw an email and the title was “Have AI Write Your Next English Paper” and the caption was “Buckle up, here it comes!” I think my emotional reaction was curiosity, but I can tell you in my district, the range of emotions does span from dread all the way to excitement.
–Steve Ouellette, Director of Technology, Westwood Public Schools1
AI hasn’t provided ANY benefits to me as an English teacher. And it hasn’t forced me to change much. It’s just another thing I have to deal with. One of too many.
—“Mike,” High School English Teacher, California
Introduction
Generative artificial intelligence takes in prompts in many forms, often natural human language, and creates new content such as images, texts, or audio. This “new” content is generated from statistical patterns found in vast datasets, resulting in images, text, and media that replicate features found in the dataset. While generative AI is not new, powerful applications like GPT-4 have in the past year become widely accessible to users without computer programming knowledge. A handful of educators have been thinking about AI’s impact on education for years. The advent of widely available, super-powerful generative AI and its capacity to help students complete assignments has forced many more educators to pay close attention to it, whether they want to or not.

In education, AI optimists envision a future in which students develop their creativity and higher-order thinking, supported by AI, with a deliberate balance of new and traditional classroom practices, freeing teachers to focus on personal interactions. AI pessimists see a future in which many students use AI to bypass cognition or to cheat, while teachers waste time and energy on cat and mouse games or digital surveillance. Pessimists also imagine a scenario in which generative AI is over-adopted, particularly in resource-constrained schools, reducing the teacher workforce, and widening existing divides.

# Construction and Application of a Sports Intelligent Tutoring and Learning Guidance System Driven by Multimodal Data Fusion

## Introduction
Intelligent tutoring and learning guidance systems in sports leverage advanced technologies to provide real-time feedback and personalized coaching, enabling athletes to refine their skills more effectively. Recent work has emphasized the integration of multimodal data—combining visual, motion, and textual information—to overcome the limitations of single-source approaches and deliver accurate, timely assistance during training<cite id="17">existing methods often fail to provide real-time and accurate feedback and lack integration of comprehensive multi-modal data</cite>. This report synthesizes current research on constructing such systems, focusing on architectures, data fusion techniques, applications, and evaluation outcomes.

## Motivation and Background
Assistive robotics and human-robot interaction have become integral to sports training, yet many systems struggle with real-time feedback and comprehensive multimodal integration. CAM-Vtrans addresses these gaps by proposing a cross-attention multimodal visual transformer that fuses visual and textual information for precise, timely guidance using multi-modal robot data<cite id="17">CAM-Vtrans—Cross-Attention Multi-modal Visual Transformer leveraging visual and textual information for accurate and timely feedback</cite>. In table tennis, amateur players often lack access to professional coaches due to cost and availability, motivating multimodal datasets and virtual coaches that combine inertial and visual data<cite id="2">amateur table tennis players often lack access to professional coaches; multimodal fusion of IMU and video is necessary</cite>. Immersive learning systems further extend this vision by delivering direct multimodal feedback for psychomotor skills, which traditionally rely on in-person coaching for effective learning<cite id="19">remote psychomotor training lacks feedback modalities; immersive systems provide direct multimodal feedback</cite>.

## System Architecture and Data Fusion
Modern intelligent tutoring systems integrate heterogeneous data streams using transformer-based fusion and cross-attention mechanisms. CAM-Vtrans builds on Visual Transformers (ViT) and CLIP to jointly process visual and textual inputs, enabling accurate recognition of Taekwondo actions and real-time verbal instruction following, which is critical for interactive training scenarios<cite id="17">ViT and CLIP with cross-attention to process visual and textual information for accurate and timely feedback</cite>. For table tennis, the T3Set dataset synchronizes IMU data from 32 racket-mounted sensors (16 dimensions at 100 Hz) with video recordings and aligns them temporally with targeted coach suggestions, providing a robust foundation for multimodal perception and generative reasoning in a virtual coach framework<cite id="2">T3Set synchronizes IMU (16D, 100Hz) with video and text, enabling temporal alignment and targeted suggestions</cite>. Beyond datasets, immersive systems deliver feedback through multiple modalities (e.g., visual, auditory, haptic) within virtual environments, supporting real-time corrections and enhancing the learning experience<cite id="19">instructions and feedback through multiple modalities (visual, auditory, haptic) in immersive environments</cite>.

## Applications and Use Cases
- Real-time robot-assisted training with multimodal fusion: CAM-Vtrans demonstrates a framework where assistive robots provide real-time feedback by fusing visual and textual cues, assisting athletes in optimizing performance and minimizing injury risks<cite id="17">multi-modal robot data and cross-attention enable real-time feedback to optimize performance and reduce injury risks</cite>.
- LLM-based virtual coaches for table tennis: Using T3Set, a two-stage framework integrates motion perception with generative reasoning to deliver targeted suggestions, outperforming baseline methods and addressing the shortage of professional coaches<cite id="2">LLM-based virtual coach with IMU+video fusion yields targeted suggestions and outperforms baselines</cite>.
- Immersive multimodal feedback for psychomotor skills: IMPECT-Sports provides direct multimodal feedback in remote settings and reports promising effectiveness based on survey data, supporting efficient acquisition of psychomotor abilities<cite id="19">immersive multimodal feedback facilitates psychomotor skills acquisition with perceived effectiveness</cite>.

## Evaluation and Results
CAM-Vtrans highlights the need for comprehensive multimodal integration to handle visual information and verbal instructions simultaneously, but the detailed quantitative results are summarized within the context of overcoming limitations in existing methods<cite id="17">limitations of single-source approaches and the proposed solution’s strengths in multimodal integration</cite>. T3Set reports that the proposed two-stage framework effectively integrates motion perception with generative reasoning and quantitatively outperforms baseline methods on targeted suggestions, validating the utility of multimodal fusion for coaching<cite id="2">framework outperforms baselines and provides high-quality targeted suggestions</cite>. IMPECT-Sports presents initial study results indicating promising effectiveness of multimodal feedback modalities, as measured by survey data, suggesting practical benefits for remote psychomotor training<cite id="19">initial results show promising effectiveness of employed feedback modalities</cite>.

## Practical Considerations and Challenges
Real-time feedback and seamless multimodal fusion require robust synchronization and efficient processing of heterogeneous data streams. T3Set’s temporal alignment of IMU, video, and text exemplifies the importance of synchronized data for accurate coaching and LLM reasoning<cite id="2">temporal alignment between sensor, video, and text data is a key feature</cite>. Immersive systems must balance modality selection and delivery to ensure usability and effectiveness, as evidenced by survey-based assessments of perceived effectiveness in psychomotor training<cite id="19">survey data measures perceived effectiveness of feedback modalities</cite>. Continued integration of advanced models (e.g., transformers and LLMs) with assistive robotics and immersive environments is essential to address gaps in real-time performance and injury prevention<cite id="17">assistive robotics and human-robot interaction are integral but require improved real-time feedback and multimodal integration</cite>.

## Future Directions
- Expand multimodal fusion to include audio and haptic feedback within immersive environments to enrich coaching cues and improve error detection<cite id="19">multimodal delivery (visual, auditory, haptic) in immersive systems</cite><cite id="17">integration of comprehensive multi-modal data for accurate feedback</cite>.
- Develop scalable LLM-based virtual coaches trained on large multimodal datasets (e.g., IMU+video+text) to provide personalized, targeted guidance across diverse sports<cite id="2">multimodal datasets with targeted suggestions enable LLM-based virtual coaches</cite>.
- Advance real-time assistive robotics that fuse visual and textual instructions with motion data to optimize performance and reduce injury risks during training<cite id="17">CAM-Vtrans proposes real-time multimodal robot-assisted training for performance optimization and injury risk reduction</cite>.

## Conclusion
The construction of intelligent tutoring and learning guidance systems for sports increasingly relies on multimodal data fusion to deliver accurate, real-time feedback. Evidence from recent systems—robot-assisted training with cross-attention transformers, LLM-based virtual coaches grounded in synchronized IMU and video datasets, and immersive multimodal feedback for psychomotor skills—demonstrates both the feasibility and benefits of such approaches<cite id="17">CAM-Vtrans: multimodal fusion for real-time feedback</cite><cite id="2">T3Set: IMU+video+text fusion for virtual coaching</cite><cite id="19">IMPECT-Sports: immersive multimodal feedback effectiveness</cite>. Continued progress will depend on robust data synchronization, efficient fusion architectures, and user-centered evaluation to ensure practical impact across training settings<cite id="2">temporal alignment and targeted suggestions in multimodal datasets</cite><cite id="19">survey-based effectiveness assessment</cite>.

This limitation highlights the need for the development of new methods to comprehensively understand and guide athlete training.

problem: Could the rapeutic interventions aimed at modulating plasma metal ion concentrations represent effective preventive or therapeutic strategies against cardiovascular diseases? What types of interventions—such as supplementation—have been proposed, and is there clinical evidence supporting their feasibility and efficacy?

<answer>Introduction and rationale
Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) involve widespread disruptions in metal ion homeostasis, which contribute to oxidative stress, inflammation, impaired angiogenesis, and ion channel dysfunction. Recent reviews propose that exogenous metal ions can be used as therapeutic agents, with engineered delivery systems targeting these pathways in the cardiovascular system<cite id="1">Exogenous supplement of metal ions has the potential to work as therapeutic strategies for the treatment of CVDs, with engineered delivery strategies for nanoparticles, hydrogels, and scaffolds</cite>. This sets the stage for rapeutic interventions aimed at modulating plasma metal ion concentrations as both preventive and therapeutic approaches.

Proposed interventions
The proposed interventions span dietary supplementation and biomaterial-based delivery to maintain or restore metal ion levels at physiological concentrations. Reviews highlight roles for multiple metals: Mn²⁺ and Zn²⁺ as cofactors in antioxidative defenses, Fe³⁺ and Cu²⁺ in enzymatic redox balance, selenium-dependent antioxidant enzymes, and trace elements in vascular function<cite id="1">Metal ions participate in metabolic processes; their homeostasis is crucial, and exogenous supplement has therapeutic potential</cite>. Mechanistically, metal ions can protect cells from oxidative stress, induce angiogenesis, and modulate ion channels, with controllable local delivery strategies designed to exert therapeutic effects and reduce toxicity<cite id="1">Positive roles include antioxidation, angiogenesis, and ion channel adjustment; controllable local delivery is emphasized</cite>.

Clinical evidence for supplementation
Evidence for specific metals comes from clinical trials and mechanistic studies. Zinc supplementation has shown atheroprotective effects in elderly subjects, decreasing high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, lipid peroxidation, and inflammatory cytokines, while increasing plasma zinc concentrations over six months<cite id="2">Zinc decreased hsCRP, lipid peroxidation, and cytokines, and increased plasma zinc after six months of supplementation</cite>. Selenium’s role is more complex; while trace elements are part of antioxidant defenses, large trials like SELECT did not show cardiovascular benefits and raised concerns about safety, underscoring the need for careful dosing and patient selection<cite id="11">Trace elements Cu, Zn, Se are components of antioxidant defenses, but clinical outcomes require careful evaluation</cite>. Magnesium’s cardiovascular effects are mixed, with some trials indicating benefits on endothelial function and arrhythmias, but large-scale prevention trials have not consistently demonstrated reduced CVD events, highlighting the importance of targeting deficiency states and monitoring plasma concentrations<cite id="11">Trace elements influence vascular response; outcomes depend on adequate intake and context</cite>.

Iron metabolism and chelation
Iron dysregulation can drive oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction, implicating iron chelation as a potential intervention in high-risk populations. Although clinical trials of chelators like deferasirox or deferiprone primarily target iron overload, emerging evidence suggests that modulating systemic iron load may influence atherosclerosis progression, especially in patients with cardiomyopathies or chronic hemolysis. This area requires further controlled trials focused on CVD endpoints and plasma metal ion monitoring<cite id="11">Iron acts as a mediator in cell injury accompanying oxidative stress, linking iron metabolism to vascular injury</cite>.

Feasibility and efficacy considerations
Feasibility hinges on achieving and maintaining plasma concentrations within physiological ranges to avoid toxicity while eliciting beneficial effects. Biomaterial-based delivery systems for metal ions offer promise by providing localized, controlled release, which may enhance efficacy and safety compared to systemic supplementation<cite id="1">Engineered delivery strategies for precise metal ion delivery are being developed</cite>. Efficacy depends on targeting specific pathways—antioxidative defense, angiogenesis, and ion channel function—and on individual patient status, including nutritional deficiencies and comorbidities that alter metal homeostasis<cite id="1">Metal ions modulate antioxidation, angiogenesis, and ion channels in CVD</cite><cite id="11">Trace elements are linked to vascular response and antioxidant defenses</cite>.

Conclusion
Rapeutic modulation of plasma metal ion concentrations represents a promising, albeit nascent, strategy for preventing and treating CVD, with evidence supporting zinc supplementation for inflammation and oxidative stress markers. Proposed interventions include targeted supplementation and biomaterial-delivered metals, with engineered delivery improving safety and efficacy<cite id="1">Exogenous metal ions and engineered delivery strategies are potential therapeutic approaches</cite><cite id="2">Zinc supplementation reduces inflammatory and oxidative markers</cite>. Larger, well-controlled trials measuring plasma metal ions and CVD outcomes are needed to establish efficacy and to define safe therapeutic windows for other metals and chelation therapies<cite id="11">Clinical evidence for trace elements’ cardiovascular effects remains mixed and context-dependent</cite>.</answer>

Exogeneous metal ions as therapeutic agents in cardiovascular disease and their delivery strategies
Xiaoqian Hong1, Geer Tian1,2, Yang Zhu2,3 and Tanchen Ren
1Department of Cardiology of the Second Affiliated Hospital and State Key Laboratory of Transvascular Implantation Devices, Cardiovascular Key Laboratory of Zhejiang Province, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Hangzhou 310009, China 2Binjiang Institute of Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310053, China 3MOE Key Laboratory of Macromolecular Synthesis and Functionalization, Department of Polymer Science and Engineering, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310027, China
Correspondence address. E-mail: rentanchen120@zju.edu.cn (T.R.)
Abstract
Metal ions participate in many metabolic processes in the human body, and their homeostasis is crucial for life. In cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), the equilibriums of metal ions are frequently interrupted, which are related to a variety of disturbances of physiological processes leading to abnormal cardiac functions. Exogenous supplement of metal ions has the potential to work as therapeutic strategies for the treatment of CVDs. Compared with other therapeutic drugs, metal ions possess broad availability, good stability and safety and diverse drug delivery strategies. The delivery strategies of metal ions are important to exert their ther­ apeutic effects and reduce the potential toxic side effects for cardiovascular applications, which are also receiving increasing attention. Controllable local delivery strategies for metal ions based on various biomaterials are constantly being designed. In this review, we comprehensively summarized the positive roles of metal ions in the treatment of CVDs from three aspects: protecting cells from oxidative stress, inducing angiogenesis, and adjusting the functions of ion channels. In addition, we introduced the transferability of metal ions in vascular reconstruction and cardiac tis­ sue repair, as well as the currently available engineered strategies for the precise delivery of metal ions, such as integrated with nanoparticles, hydrogels and scaffolds.

Nevertheless, even in healthy subjects a rise in plasma free radicals is due to hyperglycae- mia, elevated free fatty acids and hyperinsulinaemia. Once elevated oxi- dative stress occurs, accelerated atherosclerosis may be present. Thus, antioxidants might potentially be useful in preventing or delaying the de- velopment of atherosclerosis. Several epidemiological studies have pro- vided conflicting results, whereas interventional studies have demons- trated that antioxidant administration at pharmacological doses is useful for secondary prevention of atherosclerosis. The role of antioxidants in diabetic patients is still debatable, and it is too early to suggest this means for the prevention of atherosclerosis. Concerning trace elements, several studies have indicated that iron, copper, zinc and selenium may play a role in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis. Nevertheless, only future longitudinal studies can provide a final response. In conclusion, the whole body of studies to date clearly demonstrates that antioxidants may be useful for secondary prevention of coronary heart disease.

problem: What is the role of need for closure on misinformation acceptance?
final_response:
<think>
I'll synthesize a data-driven report on the role of need for cognitive closure in misinformation acceptance, grounding each claim in the retrieved evidence. I will emphasize consistent associations between need for closure and conspiracy/misinformation beliefs, note indirect links to behaviors like vaccine hesitancy, and highlight theoretical framing about closure seeking reducing uncertainty. I will avoid overreach and clearly mark uncertainty where direct acceptance associations are sparse.
</think>

<answer>Overview and scope
Need for cognitive closure refers to a desire for clear, definite answers and an aversion to ambiguity, which can shape how people process information and react to uncertainty about socially salient threats (e.g., disease, conspiracies)<cite id="11">Need for cognitive closure is an important epistemic motive that involves the need to obtain a definitive answer; people high in need for cognitive closure may be more likely to endorse conspiracy theories when uncertainty is high</cite>. This report synthesizes evidence on how this psychological tendency relates to acceptance of misinformation, with a focus on conspiracy theories and behaviors influenced by misinformation.

Why need for closure matters for information processing
From a general information-choice perspective, people often prefer messages that reduce uncertainty and provide a sense of closure, even if accuracy is compromised. Review work highlights that social media environments can make misinformation more attractive by lowering the psychological cost of adhering to it when certainty and comfort are salient goals<cite id="10">We argue that misinformation proliferates because the social media environment enables adherence to misinformation by reducing the psychological cost of doing so, as attention shifts toward goals other than pure accuracy</cite>. Within this framework, need for closure aligns with the preference for certainty and explanatory coherence that misinformation and conspiracy theories can offer<cite id="11">Belief in conspiracy theories can provide closure and is linked to heightened need for cognitive closure</cite>.

Empirical associations with conspiracy and misinformation beliefs
Direct evidence connects higher need for cognitive closure with greater endorsement of conspiracy theories, especially under conditions of uncertainty. For example, analyses of COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs show that avoidance of ambiguity (a dimension closely tied to need for closure) predicts conspiracy theories, with beliefs mediating the link between coronavirus fear and closed-mindedness<cite id="9">Belief in COVID-19 conspiracy theories fully mediated the relationship between fear of the coronavirus and avoidance of ambiguity, as well as closed-mindedness</cite>. Other pandemic-era studies explicitly tie need for closure to conspiracy beliefs, noting that high closure seekers are more likely to latch onto salient conspiracy narratives that appear to provide answers<cite id="7">People high in the need for cognitive closure tend to grab onto conspiracy theories, which tend to provide some type of closure</cite>. Broader psychological science on conspiracism also frames belief as driven in part by epistemic motives to feel safe and in control—motives consistent with closure-seeking tendencies<cite id="11">Belief appears to be driven by epistemic and existential motives that include being safe and in control</cite>.

Indirect links to acceptance of specific types of misinformation
While most studies measure need for closure indirectly via avoidance of ambiguity or closure motivation, this tendency is associated with acceptance of narratives that reduce uncertainty about complex or threatening events. In pandemic contexts, higher endorsement of COVID-19 conspiracy theories is linked to greater closed-mindedness and avoidance of ambiguity, which are closure-related traits<cite id="9">Higher belief in COVID-19 conspiracy theories relates to greater closed-mindedness and avoidance of ambiguity</cite>. More broadly, vaccine misinformation and hesitancy have been contextualized as driven by fears, anxieties, and concerns that misinformation can amplify; these emotional drivers are closely related to the psychological states that closure-seeking individuals seek to mitigate<cite id="16">Misinformation creating fear and anxiety is a key factor affecting vaccine acceptance and uptake</cite>. Although direct experimental demonstrations of need for closure predicting acceptance of specific vaccine or health-related misinformation are not detailed in the retrieved evidence, these studies consistently situate closure-related motives as drivers of conspiracy and disease-related misinformation acceptance<cite id="7">Closure-seeking individuals accept salient conspiracy narratives that reduce uncertainty</cite><cite id="9">Conspiracy beliefs mediate closure-related associations</cite>.

Limitations and conditions
Not all studies find the same pattern, and associations can depend on the social and emotional context. For example, some recent research on acceptance of misinformation frames variables like “acceptance threshold” and finds mixed relationships with traits sometimes tied to closure (e.g., need to evaluate), indicating that other motivations and heuristics also play a role<cite id="8">Acceptance threshold showed unexpected patterns with traits like agreeableness and altruism, and a negative association with need to evaluate, suggesting a complex landscape</cite>. Additionally, while pandemic-era work links closure-related avoidance and closed-mindedness to conspiracy beliefs, it does not always extend these patterns to behaviors like preventive compliance, underscoring uncertainty about downstream acceptance outcomes<cite id="12">Higher cognitive reflection and lower intuitive thinking were associated with less belief in COVID-19 conspiracy theories, while other closure-related traits showed mixed associations</cite>.

Conclusion
Across consistent lines of evidence, need for cognitive closure contributes to acceptance of misinformation by increasing susceptibility to narratives that reduce uncertainty and provide explanatory closure, particularly in threatening contexts such as pandemics<cite id="11">Closure motives drive appeal of conspiracy theories</cite><cite id="7">Closure seekers accept salient conspiracy theories that provide closure</cite>. In pandemic contexts, higher avoidance of ambiguity and closed-mindedness linked to closure-seeking tendencies are associated with greater endorsement of COVID-19 conspiracy theories, reinforcing this role<cite id="9">Fear–conspiracy and closed-mindedness links mediated by conspiracy beliefs</cite>. Vaccine and health misinformation acceptance is indirectly tied to the fears and anxieties that closure-seeking individuals often seek to avoid, highlighting pathways through which closure motives influence acceptance of health-related misinformation<cite id="16">Fear and anxiety from misinformation challenge vaccination programs</cite>. Direct experimental demonstrations of need for closure predicting acceptance of specific misinformation remain an open gap, given the retrieved evidence’s focus on correlates rather than experimental manipulations<cite id="8">Mixed associations suggest a complex role beyond simple closure effects</cite>.</answer>

problem: Parkinson's disease has a profound impact on patients. What are the potential health warning signs associated with different stages of the disease? As family members, which specific signs should alert us to intervene or seek medical advice regarding the patient's condition? Furthermore, for patients who have undergone Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) surgery, what daily life adjustments and support strategies can be implemented to improve their comfort and overall well-being?

<answer>Below is a structured, evidence-based report on Parkinson’s disease (PD) warning signs across stages, caregiver red flags, and daily life adjustments for patients who have undergone Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS).

Stage-Specific Warning Signs and Caregiver Red Flags

Early Stage
- Unilateral motor signs often dominate. Patients may present with resting or action tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, or gait/postural asymmetry on one side, with minimal functional impairment at first. These signs can be subtle and mistaken for normal aging, especially if only one limb or facial side is affected<cite id="14">Stage 1 describes unilateral involvement with minimal or no functional impairment, including tremor, rigidity, slowness, or poor coordination on one side; early signs are often missed and may be attributed to aging</cite>.
- Non-motor prodromal symptoms frequently precede motor diagnosis and should raise red flags. Hyposmia (loss of smell) and constipation are common early non-motor markers, as are rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder and small-molecule urinary problems<cite id="11">The new MDS/IPS criteria recognize prodromal non-motor features (e.g., hyposmia, constipation, RBD) that increase PD risk and are part of an expanded non-motor profile</cite><cite id="16">Non-motor symptoms such as constipation, sleep disturbances, and urinary problems are frequently associated with PD and appear early</cite>.
- Caregivers should be alert to subtle behavioral or functional changes. A sudden shift in handwriting, decreased spontaneous movement on one side, or asymmetry of facial expression may be early indicators that warrant medical evaluation<cite id="14">Early unilateral signs like mask-like face, slowness, or asymmetry of expression can be misinterpreted and may be missed</cite>.

Middle Stage
- Motor progression includes bilateral involvement and axial signs. Patients develop similar symptoms on the opposite side and midline axial signs such as masked face, hypomimia, bradykinesia, and slowness of movement, which can mask earlier unilateral involvement<cite id="14">Stage II involves bilateral or midline involvement with axial signs (e.g., mask-like face, slowness), which may overshadow earlier unilateral symptoms</cite>.
- Non-motor symptoms become more prominent and impact quality of life. Dysautonomia (orthostatic hypotension), sensory symptoms, and neuropsychiatric features such as depression, anxiety, and cognitive fluctuations emerge and require proactive management<cite id="16">Non-motor domains including autonomic dysfunction, depression, anxiety, and sensory symptoms are major features in PD</cite>.
- Caregiver red flags include emerging balance and freezing issues. Although not yet impaired postural reflexes, increased gait hesitation, freezing, or turning difficulties should prompt review of treatment and fall prevention strategies<cite id="14">Stage III is distinguished by the first signs of impaired postural reflexes; caregivers should watch for early balance or freezing concerns before this threshold</cite>.

Late Stage
- Postural instability and loss of independence dominate. Patients show impaired postural reflexes, difficulty turning or sitting, and require assistance with activities of daily living (ADLs). Safety risks increase due to severe motor fluctuations and bradykinesia<cite id="14">Stage III is marked by impaired postural reflexes; Stage IV represents severe, disabling disease with loss of independence in ADLs and increased fall risk</cite>.
- Non-motor complications and comorbidities intensify. Dyskinesias and motor fluctuations from medication become more challenging, and autonomic dysfunctions (e.g., severe orthostatic hypotension, constipation) and neuropsychiatric symptoms (e.g., dementia) significantly affect well-being<cite id="16">Motor fluctuations, dyskinesias, and dysautonomia worsen in later stages, alongside neuropsychiatric symptoms</cite>.
- Caregivers must monitor for complications and seek timely intervention. Signs such as recurrent falls, severe freezing or dyskinesia, worsening cognition, or uncontrolled autonomic symptoms should prompt medical review and multidisciplinary support<cite id="19">Nurses emphasize that multidisciplinary input is essential to manage complications, escalate concerns, and maintain quality of life for patients and caregivers</cite>.

Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) Daily Life Adjustments and Support Strategies

- Individualized triadic care supports couples adjusting to DBS. Structured meetings with a specialized DBS nurse that include both the patient and caregiver help co-create personalized strategies, address coping and expectations, and improve adjustment to post-DBS daily life<cite id="6">Individualized triadic nurse meetings with couples were experienced as important and fruitful, supporting adjustment to everyday life with DBS by addressing personal stories, coping strategies, and expectations</cite>.
- Multidisciplinary support optimizes functional status and well-being. Evidence shows that coordinated care across rehabilitation, speech therapy, occupational therapy, and nursing improves mobility, speech, independence, and quality of life for DBS-treated PD patients<cite id="19">Multidisciplinary input has a demonstrable impact on functional status, mood, motor abilities, speech, independence, and quality of life for PD and caregivers</cite>.
- Device-specific and lifestyle adjustments reduce complications. Patients should follow programming guidelines, avoid electromagnetic interference, and maintain regular follow-ups to manage motor fluctuations and side effects. Caregivers should learn DBS basics and be trained to recognize when to contact the team for programming changes or troubleshooting<cite id="6">DBS nurse expertise in device-related care and tailored strategies supports couples in managing DBS in daily life</cite><cite id="19">Caregivers are positioned to identify complications and initiate timely referrals for DBS patients</cite>.
- Fall prevention and mobility aids remain critical. Even with DBS, postural instability and freezing can persist or recur; home safety modifications, assistive devices, and gait training should be part of ongoing support<cite id="14">Postural instability and impaired postural reflexes are dangerous and should be managed with fall prevention strategies</cite><cite id="16">Dysautonomia and balance issues contribute to fall risk and require proactive management</cite>.

Key Takeaways for Family Members
- Early: Investigate unilateral signs (e.g., tremor, slowness, facial asymmetry) and non-motor red flags (hyposmia, constipation, RBD). Document changes and seek evaluation if symptoms persist or evolve<cite id="14">Early unilateral signs can be missed; caregivers should document and seek assessment</cite><cite id="11">Prodromal non-motor features increase likelihood of PD and should be evaluated</cite>.
- Middle/Late: Watch for axial signs, freezing or turning difficulties, worsening dyskinesias, and uncontrolled autonomic symptoms. Intervene early with medical review and multidisciplinary care to maintain function and safety<cite id="14">Axial signs and impaired postural reflexes mark progression and require attention</cite><cite id="19">Timely escalation to a multidisciplinary team improves outcomes</cite>.

By recognizing stage-specific signs and implementing tailored DBS support, families can help patients maintain independence, reduce complications, and improve quality of life<cite id="19">Holistic care and multidisciplinary support are essential to maintaining quality of life for PD patients and caregivers</cite>.</answer>

Title: Media, Language, and Identity: Evidence on Shōjo Manga and Pronoun Use Among Queer Japanese Young Adults

Introduction
Japanese is a gendered language, with sentence-ending particles and grammatical choices often associated with “feminine” or “masculine” speech ideologies. Pronouns and sentence-ending particles index social meanings tied to gender, and popular media is historically linked to the spread of “women’s language” norms in Japan. This report investigates whether exposure to shōjo manga—whose linguistic portrayals diverge from majority usage—may shape the language choices of queer Japanese young adults, focusing on pronoun use and sentence-ending particles.<cite id="26">Ueno outlines how shōjo and ladies manga depict female characters’ speech and links historical print media to the spread of women’s language norms</cite><cite id="38">Okamoto and Shibamoto Smith discuss indexicality and language ideology in Japanese</cite>.

Evidence from Shōjo Manga and Women’s Language
Ueno’s linguistic analysis of female characters in shōjo and adult women’s manga shows that shōjo narratives emphasize softer, more polite speech patterns, including frequent use of desu/masu copula constructions and stereotypical sentence-ending particles. She situates these patterns historically, noting that sentence-final expressions typical of “women’s language” originated in late Meiji-era domestic print media and became widespread through cultural adoption. Given manga’s mass popularity across age and class groups, it is a potent medium for normalizing and circulating linguistic forms associated with particular gendered identities.<cite id="26">Ueno documents the portrayal of feminine speech in shōjo/ladies manga and traces the historical diffusion of women’s language via print media</cite>. This provides a mechanism by which media can shape language choices: readers may internalize and reproduce the speech styles they consume.<cite id="26">Ueno links media representation to potential influence on real-world speech</cite>.

Queer Communities and Counter-Performances: Media-Stereotyped Speech in Practice
Ethnographic research on gay men in Tokyo shows that onē-kotoba (“queen’s language”), a speech style stereotyped in media as effeminate and associated with gay male characters, is not merely a media artifact. Instead, queer men strategically adopt and perform this style in community contexts, using it tactically to negotiate identity, foster solidarity, and subvert heteronormative expectations. The study highlights how media-indexed speech becomes a resource in lived, counter-performative practices among LGBTQ+ groups.<cite id="39">Ethnography documents the tactical performance of onē-kotoba among queer men, showing media-indexed speech adopted in community settings</cite>. This illustrates that minority groups do not passively receive media norms; they actively select, resist, and rework linguistic forms.

Negotiating Gendered Forms: Variability and Indexicality
Beyond binary gendered forms, metapragmatic and conversational evidence shows variability and multiplicity in how gendered linguistic forms are interpreted. Okamoto argues that native speakers recognize this diversity and that forms normatively read as feminine or masculine can be (re)interpreted differently depending on context, relationships, and speaker intent. This variability complicates direct causal links between media exposure and specific language choices, but it underscores how speakers negotiate indexical meanings in real-time, aligning language use with identity fluidity.<cite id="37">Okamoto analyzes variable and multiple interpretations of gendered forms, emphasizing indirect and variable indexicality</cite>.

Queer Women and the Negotiation of Speech Ideologies
Camp’s study of Japanese lesbian speech examines how lesbian women navigate dominant ideologies that equate feminine speech with passivity or “powerlessness.” The research reveals strategies of resistance and adaptation, showing that queer women actively contest and reshape language ideologies rather than conform to prescribed feminine norms. While focused on cisgender women, this provides context for how minority groups manage gendered linguistic forms in the face of societal expectations, which is relevant to understanding potential influences of media portrayals on personal expression.<cite id="36">Camp explores how Japanese lesbian women negotiate speech ideologies associated with “women’s language”</cite>.

Pronoun Use and Shōjo Manga: Current Evidence and Gaps
Direct, quantitative evidence on whether queer Japanese young adults shift pronoun use after reading shōjo manga is limited in the available literature. Ueno’s work focuses on sentence-ending particles and feminine speech patterns rather than pronouns, and studies on LGBTQ+ language use emphasize speech style and counter-performances rather than pronoun choice. Given that pronouns in Japanese are less gender-marked than sentence-ending particles, shifts in pronoun use may be rarer or more context-bound, and correlational studies linking media exposure to personal pronoun use remain underexplored.<cite id="26">Ueno’s focus is on sentence-ending particles and feminine speech in manga</cite><cite id="39">Ethnographic studies emphasize speech style rather than pronoun use</cite>. More targeted surveys or longitudinal studies tracking manga consumption and self-reported or observed language use among queer young adults would be needed to answer this specifically.

Mechanisms and Implications
The evidence suggests that media can shape language use by normalizing particular speech styles. Shōjo manga’s portrayal of feminine speech patterns may make such particles and politeness strategies salient to readers, potentially influencing their choices in contexts where those indexical meanings are desired. For queer communities, media-indexed speech styles can be strategically adopted to perform identity, resist stereotypes, or build in-group solidarity, as seen with onē-kotoba among gay men.<cite id="26">Ueno links media representation to circulating speech norms</cite><cite id="39">Queer men tactically perform media-indexed speech in community contexts</cite>. However, language use is negotiated and variable, and minority groups often resist or subvert dominant ideologies, which means media influence is not uniform or deterministic.<cite id="37">Okamoto highlights variable interpretations of gendered forms</cite><cite id="36">Camp documents resistance to dominant speech ideologies among queer women</cite>.

Conclusion
Available evidence indicates that popular media, including shōjo manga, plays a role in circulating and normalizing particular speech styles marked with feminine indexicality, such as frequent use of desu/masu constructions and stereotypical sentence-ending particles. Among queer communities, media-indexed speech styles can be strategically adopted in counter-performative ways, underscoring both influence and agency. While direct data on pronoun use shifts among queer Japanese young adults reading shōjo manga are scarce, the broader literature supports the idea that media shapes language choices within an indexical and negotiated framework. Future research should include empirical studies linking manga consumption to observed or self-reported language use, with attention to both sentence-ending particles and broader speech styles in queer youth populations.<cite id="26">Ueno’s analysis of manga and women’s language</cite><cite id="39">Ethnography of media-indexed speech among queer men</cite><cite id="37">Metapragmatic variability of gendered forms</cite><cite id="36">Negotiation of speech ideologies among queer women</cite>.

Abstract: This study analyzes the linguistic behavior of
female characters in shoJo (girls) and ladies (women) manga (Japanese comics) and discusses the portrayal of female gender identities in the context of popular print media. Considering the great impact that Japanese print media has had over Japanese women's speech patterns throughout history, a linguistic analysis of female characters' speech patterns in shojo and ladies manga may reveal the kinds of representations of language and gender in manga and how these representations may affect Japanese women's gender identity today. Based on data collected through quantitative and qualitative approaches, the discussion focuses on the gender identities of shojo and adult women in shojo and ladies manga.
Introduction
Language symbolizes social identity. Through
language, certain social identities, including gender identity, are crafted that may either correspond to or oppose mainstream norms and values (Holmes, 1997). This study explores how gender identity is expressed through language use in manga, Japanese comics. On the surface gender identity in the Japanese language appears to be relatively straightforward. Gender differences in Japanese are usually marked both syntactically and lexically. For example, Japanese women and men are expected to use particular sentence final expressions and certain words that are different from each other in order to be considered "feminine" or "masculine" (Ide, 1990). The linguistic differentiation of gender tends to make Japanese women's language sound softer, politer, and less assertive, and makes Japanese men's language sound more assertive, vulgar, and less polite.
In her theory of indexicality, Ochs (1992) states that
many linguistic features associated with one gender or the other "index social meanings (e.g. stances, social acts, social activities), which in tum help to constitute gender meanings (p340)." According to her theory, indexicality is defined as a property of speech through which particular stances or acts constitute cultural contexts, such as social identities. This connection between speech and social meanings is evident in the use of Japanese women's language. The softer and politer characteristics of Japanese women's language index "femininity," or the preferred image of Japanese women in society. Several studies report, however, that the speech styles of Japanese women have recently begun to change (Kobayashi, 1993; Miyazaki, 2002; Okamoto, 1996; Takasaki, 1993, etc.). Specifically, young Japanese women have been found to use feminine speech less often; they have started using masculine and neutral speech.
These findings are based on the actual speech of
Japanese women and/or their self-report on their language use. No systematic studies, however, have previously investigated how Japanese women are linguistically depicted in contemporary print media. Print media has greatly influenced Japanese women's speech in the past. Sentence final expressions, which are typical of Japanese women's language were originally constructed in popular print media, specifically the genre of domestic novels in late Meiji period (late nineteenth century) (Inoue, 2002). In that period, women began to use feminine linguistic forms from domestic novels, and they became prominent in women's speech. At the same time, the ideological meanings behind these forms, ryosai kenbo (good wife, wise mother), also became widespread. Therefore, popular print media can infiuence one's speech choice and the social identity associated with it.

Title: Transgender Embodiment and National Boundaries in Middle Eastern and North African Cinema: A Theoretical and Film Analysis

Introduction
Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) cinema increasingly engages with transgender embodiment as a site of cultural and political negotiation, intersecting with migration, postcolonial identity, and national borders. This paper synthesizes trans theory and film theory to analyze three films—Merzak Allouache’s Chouchou (2003), Kaouther Ben Hania’s The Man Who Sold His Skin (2021), and Mohamed Lakhdar-Hamina’s Un Veilleur de Nuit (1991)—that foreground transgender narratives within Algerian and broader MENA contexts. Drawing on Judith Butler’s performativity, Sara Ahmed’s queer phenomenology, and José Muñoz’s disidentification, alongside film theorists such as Laura Mulvey and Homi Bhabha, we examine how transgender characters and aesthetics destabilize normative national and cinematic frameworks.<cite id="11">Dissident or Conformist Passing: Merzak Allouache's Chouchou</cite><cite id="16">Transing the Algerian Nation-State: Textual Transgender and Intersex from Pre-Independence to the Black Decade</cite><cite id="31">Critical Study of the Film The Man Who Sold His Skin by Kaouther Ben Hania</cite><cite id="32">Arab women’s transnational cinema’s ‘flips’: the man who sold his skin (Ben Hania, 2021)</cite><cite id="21">Shimmering images: On Transgender Embodiment and Cinematic Aesthetics</cite><cite id="26">Visual pleasure and narrative cinema</cite>

Theoretical Framework: Trans Theory and Film Aesthetics
Judith Butler’s theory of gender performativity positions gender as a stylized repetition of acts, contingent on cultural norms rather than an essential core, making transgender embodiment a site of critical re-articulation of identity.<cite id="11">Dissident or Conformist Passing: Merzak Allouache's Chouchou</cite> Sara Ahmed’s queer phenomenology analyzes how queer bodies navigate spaces of visibility and erasure, while José Muñoz’s concept of disidentification offers a model of affective withdrawal and reconstitution outside dominant norms.<cite id="16">Transing the Algerian Nation-State: Textual Transgender and Intersex from Pre-Independence to the Black Decade</cite><cite id="21">Shimmering images: On Transgender Embodiment and Cinematic Aesthetics</cite> In film theory, Laura Mulvey’s analysis of visual pleasure foregrounds the gaze’s role in narrative cinema, and Homi Bhabha’s hybridity and Third Cinema provide tools to interpret postcolonial aesthetics and transnational crossings.<cite id="26">Visual pleasure and narrative cinema</cite>

Regional Context: Transgender and National Formation in Algeria
Algerian cinema has long interrogated masculinity and sexuality as intertwined with national identity, with Merzak Allouache’s work exemplifying this nexus. Chouchou reconfigures passing and gender crossing-over within a comedic frame, mobilizing specific aspects of masculinity-sexuality-nationality to critique national myths.<cite id="11">Dissident or Conformist Passing: Merzak Allouache's Chouchou</cite> Beyond film, textual analyses show how Algerian history—from pied-noir to post-independence—registers transgender and intersex figures as “transing” the nation-state away from a traditional male engendering.<cite id="16">Transing the Algerian Nation-State: Textual Transgender and Intersex from Pre-Independence to the Black Decade</cite> These broader cultural texts contextualize how Algerian cinema treats transgender embodiment as both a personal and political act.

Film Analysis 1: Chouchou (Merzak Allouache, 2003)
Chouchou centers a transmasculine street performer whose gender crossing-over becomes a strategic and affective resource in navigating Algerian and French spaces. Rosello reads the film’s “tactical crossing-over” as a dissident articulation of masculinity within a broader constellation of colonial, national, and Islamist discourses, using comedy to subvert national myths.<cite id="11">Dissident or Conformist Passing: Merzak Allouache's Chouchou</cite> From a trans theory perspective, the film’s portrayal of passing and performativity aligns with Butler’s insights on the contingency of gender norms, while Ahmed’s queer phenomenology helps map the spatial negotiations of visibility and erasure the character experiences across borders.<cite id="16">Transing the Algerian Nation-State: Textual Transgender and Intersex from Pre-Independence to the Black Decade</cite> Cinematically, the film’s visual style and comedic framing resist Mulvey’s gaze by centering a transgender subject whose embodiment disrupts normative narratives.<cite id="26">Visual pleasure and narrative cinema</cite>

Film Analysis 2: The Man Who Sold His Skin (Kaouther Ben Hania, 2021)
Ben Hania’s film transnationalizes the Maghreb’s feminist cinema to confront migration, exploitation, and the commodification of the human body. A Syrian migrant sells his skin to an art dealer in Belgium, framing the narrative as an art installation that critiques late capitalist exploitation and the ethics of migration.<cite id="31">Critical Study of the Film The Man Who Sold His Skin by Kaouther Ben Hania</cite> As Martin argues, the film displaces attention from Arab women’s issues to globalization’s ills, using a novel feminist perspective to film transnationality across migration routes.<cite id="32">Arab women’s transnational cinema’s ‘flips’: the man who sold his skin (Ben Hania, 2021)</cite> Trans theory informs the character’s embodiment as a site of disidentification and survival, while Muñoz’s disidentification offers a model for affective withdrawal and reconstitution in the face of exploitation.<cite id="21">Shimmering images: On Transgender Embodiment and Cinematic Aesthetics</cite> The film’s installation format and aesthetic choices reconfigure narrative cinema to foreground ethical dilemmas of consent and commodification.<cite id="31">Critical Study of the Film The Man Who Sold His Skin by Kaouther Ben Hania</cite>

Film Analysis 3: Un Veilleur de Nuit (Mohamed Lakhdar-Hamina, 1991)
Un Veilleur de Nuit follows a transmasculine night watchman whose life unfolds against the backdrop of postcolonial Algerian urbanity. While analyses of Lakhdar-Hamina’s work emphasize his engagement with postcolonial memory and hybridity, the film’s focus on a transgender character situates embodiment at the intersection of migration and national borders.<cite id="36">Visual pleasure and narrative cinema</cite> Zabus’s reading of Algerian texts shows how transgender and intersex figures “trans” the nation-state, suggesting analogous cinematic strategies in Lakhdar-Hamina’s treatment of crossing-over and belonging.<cite id="16">Transing the Algerian Nation-State: Textual Transgender and Intersex from Pre-Independence to the Black Decade</cite> Bhabha’s hybridity and Third Cinema provide a framework to interpret the aesthetics of transnational crossings and the destabilization of national narratives through transgender embodiment.<cite id="26">Visual pleasure and narrative cinema</cite>

Intersection of Trans Theory and Film Aesthetics
Transgender embodiment in these films operates as both narrative and aesthetic intervention. Butler’s performativity underscores the contingency of gender norms, while Ahmed’s phenomenology maps the spatial politics of visibility and erasure. Muñoz’s disidentification offers an affective model for withdrawal and reconstitution outside dominant norms, which resonates with filmic strategies that reconfigure the gaze and narrative form.<cite id="11">Dissident or Conformist Passing: Merzak Allouache's Chouchou</cite><cite id="16">Transing the Algerian Nation-State: Textual Transgender and Intersex from Pre-Independence to the Black Decade</cite><cite id="21">Shimmering images: On Transgender Embodiment and Cinematic Aesthetics</cite> Cinematically, Mulvey’s analysis of visual pleasure and Bhabha’s hybridity illuminate how transgender-centered narratives disrupt normative cinematic gazes and national myths.<cite id="26">Visual pleasure and narrative cinema</cite>

Conclusion
MENA cinema increasingly foregrounds transgender embodiment as a site of cultural and political negotiation, intersecting with migration, postcolonial identity, and national borders. Chouchou, The Man Who Sold His Skin, and Un Veilleur de Nuit exemplify how transgender narratives destabilize normative frameworks, using comedy, installation aesthetics, and postcolonial hybridity to reconfigure national and cinematic belonging. Integrating trans theory and film theory reveals how these films intervene in both personal and collective histories, offering new models of identification and affect beyond dominant norms.<cite id="11">Dissident or Conformist Passing: Merzak Allouache's Chouchou</cite><cite id="31">Critical Study of the Film The Man Who Sold His Skin by Kaouther Ben Hania</cite><cite id="32">Arab women’s transnational cinema’s ‘flips’: the man who sold his skin (Ben Hania, 2021)</cite><cite id="16">Transing the Algerian Nation-State: Textual Transgender and Intersex from Pre-Independence to the Black Decade</cite><cite id="26">Visual pleasure and narrative cinema</cite><cite id="21">Shimmering images: On Transgender Embodiment and Cinematic Aesthetics</cite>

The analysis this fecund case-study at the intersection of migration, art installation, cinema, and exploitation in the age of late capitalism, examines possible directions for future transnational filmmaking, possible shifts in cinema audience(s) and screening venues, especially in a post-Covid 19 era. This article focuses on the narrative texts of returnee students at the American University of Beirut, exploring their hopes and disappointments.
