problem: Research the current applications and recent scientific advancements of various light-based therapies (e.g., laser, IPL, LED) in aesthetic medicine for treating conditions such as photoaging, promoting skin whitening/brightening, and reducing hyperpigmentation (like age spots or melasma).
final_response:
<think>...
Plan: Synthesize the provided evidence into a structured, data-driven report on light-based therapies (laser, IPL, LED) for photoaging, skin whitening/brightening, and hyperpigmentation (age spots/melasma). Extract key findings from the systematic reviews and meta-analyses for melasma (picosecond and QS Nd:YAG lasers), IPL for photoaging, and LED/LLLT for skin rejuvenation. Note uncertainties and methodological limitations as reported. Avoid unsupported claims and ensure every factual statement is wrapped in a <cite> tag using the provided reference IDs.
</think>

<answer>
Light-based therapies in aesthetic medicine encompass lasers, intense pulsed light (IPL), and light-emitting diodes (LEDs), each with distinct mechanisms and clinical applications for photoaging, skin whitening/brightening, and hyperpigmentation such as age spots and melasma. A review of LED devices for skin rejuvenation notes that while interest is high, scientific support from unbiased, controlled studies is limited, and LEDs are thought to work via photomodulation rather than thermal effects to induce controlled wound healing responses<cite id="1">LED devices are thought to work by effecting photomodulation ... with few unbiased, controlled studies</cite>. A more recent narrative review of photobiomodulation (PBM) summarizes clinical evidence for skin rejuvenation and highlights methodologic flaws, small cohorts, and industry funding, while noting uncertainty about whether LED sources produce physiologic effects comparable to laser systems in higher-quality studies<cite id="42">A reasonable body of clinical trial evidence ... Methodologic flaws ... It remains unclear if light-emitting diode sources induce physiologic effects of comparable nature and magnitude to those of the laser-based systems</cite>. Systematic reviews also emphasize that LED-based photodynamic therapy (PDT) can improve skin quality, reduce wrinkles and pigmentation, and increase collagen with decreased elastin, but call for better-designed randomized controlled trials<cite id="14">Evidence supports global improvement ... increased collagen fibers and decreased elastin fibers after LED-mediated PDT ... need for well-designed randomized control trials</cite>.

For photoaging, a systematic review of IPL for skin rejuvenation evaluated 16 studies (637 participants) and concluded IPL is effective for telangiectasia, wrinkles, pores, erythema, rhytids, texture, lentigines, hyperpigmentation, and overall photoaging score, though most studies had low methodological quality and there is no consensus on parameters<cite id="33">The most studies results showed the efficacy of IPL treatment in telangiectasia, wrinkles, pore, erythema, rhytids, texture, lentigines, hyperpigmentation, and photoaging score ... Nine studies showed low methodological quality</cite>. In combination approaches, a randomized controlled trial found that using a fractional CO<sub>2</sub> laser with rhodamine-intense pulsed light (r-IPL) produced better wrinkle reduction and faster recovery than fractional CO<sub>2</sub> laser alone, with higher patient satisfaction<cite id="1">Patients treated with the combination of r-IPL and fractional CO2 laser showed better results ... with a statistically significant reduction in healing times and duration of post-treatment erythema ... higher patient satisfaction</cite>.

Regarding skin whitening and hyperpigmentation, LED/LLLT evidence is variable. The PBM review notes variable success for skin rejuvenation/anti-aging and emphasizes the need for rigorous trials, while highlighting effectiveness and tolerability across multiple dermatologic conditions<cite id="42">Skin rejuvenation and anti-aging demonstrated variable success ... Overall, the treatment was effective and well-tolerated</cite><cite id="14">LED-mediated PDT ... reduction in mottled pigmentation ... global improvement of skin quality</cite>. For melasma specifically, a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of six randomized controlled trials found that picosecond laser at 1064 nm significantly reduced MASI/mMASI with no significant side effects, whereas 755 nm picosecond laser did not significantly improve pigmentation and caused post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; efficacy of other wavelengths requires larger trials<cite id="12">Picosecond laser at 1064 nm is safe and effective ... 755 nm ... did not significantly improve the MASI/mMASI ... and caused post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation ... remains to be verified in large-scale RCTs</cite>. A network meta-analysis comparing laser-related therapies for melasma reported that QS Nd:YAG plus topical medications was superior to QS Nd:YAG alone, illustrating the potential benefit of combination approaches<cite id="13">QS-switched Nd:YAG laser + topical medications (QSND+TM) was superior to QSND</cite>. For Q-switched Nd:YAG at low fluence, a meta-analysis found no significant MASI difference versus drug monotherapy but that combining LQSNY with drugs or other lasers provided greater MASI improvement; combination with IPL also showed added benefit<cite id="20">No significant differences in MASI ... Combination therapy with LQSNY and drugs or other lasers may have pleasantly surprising efficacy ... Compared with IPL ... LQSNY with IPL provided an added benefit</cite>.

In summary, IPL shows consistent efficacy for multiple signs of photoaging with reasonable safety, albeit often in low-quality studies<cite id="33">IPL treatment is effective on skin rejuvenation ... most studies had low methodological quality</cite>. LED/LLLT offers promising but variable results for skin rejuvenation and anti-aging, with LED-based PDT showing histologic improvements in collagen and pigmentation, but calls for higher-quality trials<cite id="42">Methodologic flaws ... It remains unclear if LED effects compare to lasers</cite><cite id="14">Evidence supports global improvement ... increased collagen ... decreased elastin ... need for RCTs</cite>. For melasma, 1064 nm picosecond laser appears safe and effective in meta-analysis, while 755 nm picosecond laser may be inferior and carry hyperpigmentation risk; combination strategies with appropriate lasers or topical agents may enhance outcomes<cite id="12">1064 nm picosecond laser ... safe and effective ... 755 nm ... caused post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation</cite><cite id="13">QSND+TM superior to QSND</cite><cite id="20">Combination therapy ... provided greater MASI improvement ... added benefit with IPL</cite>.
</answer>

Their use in biology commenced in the 1950s when NASA used these devices to stimulate plant growth in space. Since that time, LEDs have been applied to a wide range of therapeutic targets, with most LEDs arranged in panels to treat large areas. The past several years in particular have seen a major interest in the use of LED devices for dermatologic therapies. While many claims have been made in a wide variety of applications, scientific support for these applications is less than robust, with few unbiased, controlled studies. This article reviews the literature in the area of nonablative skin rejuvenation using LEDs. LEDs are thought to work by effecting photomodulation, a process that attempts to modify biologic effects without inducing thermal effects. In contrast, ablative methods of skin rejuvenation remove the epidermis and induce a controlled wound healing response. Thus, both ablative and nonablative rejuvenation systems are thought to work by inducing a controlled wound healing response. True non-ablative systems are generally considered much less effective than ablative systems for wrinkle reduction and for pigmentation, but have minimal, if any, recovery time required and have a low incidence of side effects. Light-emitting diode (LED) devices are narrow band emitters of low intensity light ranging from ultraviolet (UV) through visible and into infrared. The history of LEDs dates back to the early 20 century when the first report of light-emitting diodes was published as a letter to the editor by Henry Joseph Round in the journal Electrical World in 1907. However, it was not until the 1950s that LEDs saw a utility in biology when NASA used these devices to stimulate plant growth in space. NASA research also discovered that LEDs were able to penetrate light into human tissue to promote wound healing and tissue growth (reviewed by). Since that time, LEDs have been applied to a wide range of therapeutic targets, with most LEDs arranged in panels to treat large areas. The past several years in particular have seen a major interest in the use of LED devices for dermatologic therapies. While many claims have been made in a wide variety of applications including hair growth, acne, wound healing, tissue regeneration and photo-aging, scientific support for these applications is less than robust, with few unbiased, controlled studies. This article reviews the literature in the area of nonablative skin rejuvenation using LEDs. These systems are aimed at reduction of visible blood vessels, reduction in mottled pigmentation, and reduction in wrinkles (rhytids). problem: Write a paper to discuss the influence of AI interaction on interpersonal relations, considering AI's potential to fundamentally change how and why individuals relate to each other.
final_response:
<think>

<answer>Abstract
Artificial intelligence (AI) interaction is reshaping how and why people relate to each other, with evidence spanning health, communication, and education. Relational AI can build trust and liking over time, socially assistive robots can reduce loneliness, voice-based communication fosters stronger bonds than text, and digital connectivity can both preserve and, in some contexts, hinder emotional intelligence. This paper synthesizes these findings and discusses implications for designing AI that supports meaningful human relationships.<cite id="1">Relational agents can build trust and liking over time</cite><cite id="17">Social robots reduce loneliness in older adults</cite><cite id="25">Voice-based interactions create stronger social bonds than text</cite><cite id="35">Digital connectivity can negatively influence emotional intelligence</cite>.

Introduction
AI is increasingly embedded in everyday interactions, raising questions about how these interactions alter the “how” and “why” of human relationships. Foundational work in human–computer interaction shows that socially skilled agents can cultivate long-term relational bonds, while broader reviews highlight both promise and gaps in understanding human–AI relationships. Socially assistive robots offer scalable companionship, and communication media choices shape bonding outcomes. In education, AI promises personalization but also raises concerns about social isolation and well-being. Together, these literatures suggest AI can both support and complicate interpersonal relations, depending on design, context, and usage.<cite id="7">Human–AI relationship research is emerging and cross-disciplinary</cite><cite id="1">Relational agents can build trust and liking over time</cite><cite id="17">Social robots reduce loneliness in older adults</cite><cite id="2">AI in higher education can improve efficiency but raise loneliness and technostress</cite>.

Mechanisms: Why AI Changes Relationships
AI interactions can change relationships by altering perceived agency, reciprocity, and emotional support. Relational agents designed with social-emotional skills can increase respect, liking, and trust over months of daily use, indicating that perceived authenticity and responsiveness matter for relationship quality. Systematic reviews emphasize that key constructs—agency, autonomy, reciprocity, empathy—need reconceptualization for social AI, and that methodological diversity is needed to capture dynamic processes. Ethical analyses further caution that benefits and harms coexist, depending on deployment and user context.<cite id="1">Relational agent increased respect, liking, and trust after four weeks</cite><cite id="7">Agency, autonomy, reciprocity, empathy are central; methods need diversification</cite><cite id="8">Social AI can offer companionship but poses ethical risks</cite>.

Evidence Base

Health and loneliness. Meta-analytic and umbrella review evidence indicates that socially assistive robots can improve psychosocial wellbeing, particularly for older adults. A 2025 meta-analysis of 19 studies with over 1,000 participants found that social robots significantly reduced loneliness, with larger effects in controlled conditions and in institutional settings; effects were stronger in Japan and Turkey than in the United States. These findings suggest AI companions can fill social voids when human connection is limited, but effectiveness depends on context and design.<cite id="17">Social robots significantly reduced loneliness; larger effects in institutional settings and in Japan/Turkey</cite><cite id="18">Umbrella review and meta-analysis of socially assistive robots’ impacts</cite>.

Communication mode and bonding. The choice of communication medium shapes how interactions are experienced and remembered. Field and lab experiments show that voice-based interactions create stronger social bonds and are not perceived as more awkward than richer media, whereas text is often undervalued despite its benefits for some users. Surveys of texters and talkers reveal that texting can help lonely and socially anxious individuals form close groups, but also highlight differences in relational outcomes between media users. These findings imply that AI voice interfaces may enhance relational quality, while text-centric AI may need to compensate for potential bonding gaps.<cite id="25">Voice-based interactions create stronger bonds and no more awkwardness than richer media</cite><cite id="26">Texters form close text circles; lonelier and more socially anxious than Talkers</cite>.

Education and well-being. AI in higher education can improve personalized learning and communication efficiency, but mini-reviews warn of digital fatigue, loneliness, technostress, and reduced face-to-face interactions. Over-reliance on AI may diminish interpersonal skills and emotional intelligence, leading to social isolation and anxiety. These concerns underscore the need to balance AI integration with opportunities for authentic human contact in educational settings.<cite id="2">AI in higher education can improve efficiency but raise loneliness and diminish interpersonal skills</cite>.

Digital connectivity and social-emotional development. Longitudinal and cross-sectional evidence among Generation Z students shows that digital connectivity does not necessarily harm social skills but can negatively influence emotional intelligence, particularly the ability to regulate one’s own and others’ emotions. Strong social skills, however, were positively associated with emotional intelligence, suggesting that fostering interpersonal competence can mitigate some downsides of digital interaction. These patterns imply that AI-mediated communication may require design features that promote emotional understanding and regulation.<cite id="35">Digital connectivity negatively influenced emotional intelligence; social skills enhanced emotional intelligence</cite>.

Implications for Design and Policy
The evidence suggests that AI can both support and complicate interpersonal relations. Relational agents and socially assistive robots can reduce loneliness and build trust when designed with social-emotional skills and deployed in appropriate contexts, such as institutional care. Voice-based AI interfaces may enhance bonding compared to text-only interactions, while text-centric AI should be mindful of potential bonding gaps and user loneliness. In education, AI should complement—not replace—face-to-face interactions to preserve emotional intelligence and interpersonal skills. Methodologically, future research should adopt mixed methods, longitudinal designs, and cross-cultural comparisons to capture dynamic, context-dependent effects. Ethically, frameworks should mitigate risks such as over-reliance, privacy concerns, and potential harms of social AI, especially in vulnerable populations.<cite id="1">Relational agents build trust over time</cite><cite id="17">Social robots reduce loneliness in older adults</cite><cite id="25">Voice-based interactions strengthen bonds</cite><cite id="2">AI integration must balance benefits with well-being</cite><cite id="7">Methodological diversity and reconceptualization of constructs are needed</cite><cite id="8">Ethical frameworks are necessary to address risks</cite>.

Recommendations
- Design socially skilled AI with reciprocity and responsiveness to cultivate trust over time, particularly for long-term tasks and care settings.<cite id="1">Relational agents with social-emotional skills increase liking and trust</cite>.
- Deploy socially assistive robots in institutional care, with culturally sensitive designs and control-group evaluations to maximize effectiveness.<cite id="17">Larger effects in institutional settings and cultural differences</cite>.
- Prioritize voice and video interfaces where bonding is important, while ensuring privacy and ethical safeguards; complement text-based AI with opportunities for richer interactions.<cite id="25">Voice strengthens bonds</cite><cite id="8">Ethical risks require mitigation</cite>.
- In education, integrate AI to enhance learning and communication while preserving face-to-face interactions to maintain emotional intelligence and interpersonal skills.<cite id="2">AI may diminish interpersonal skills and increase loneliness</cite><cite id="35">Social skills enhance emotional intelligence</cite>.
- Support mixed-method, longitudinal, and cross-cultural research to map how and why AI changes relationships across contexts.<cite id="7">Quantitative dominance and need for mixed methods</cite>.

Conclusion
AI interaction is changing both the mechanisms and motivations behind human relationships. Evidence from health, communication, and education indicates that well-designed AI can reduce loneliness, strengthen bonds, and enhance learning, while poorly designed or over-reliant use can erode emotional intelligence and increase isolation. A balanced, ethical, and methodologically rigorous approach is essential to harness AI’s potential to support meaningful human connections.<cite id="17">Social robots reduce loneliness</cite><cite id="25">Voice strengthens bonds</cite><cite id="2">AI can raise loneliness and diminish interpersonal skills</cite><cite id="8">Ethical risks require attention</cite>.</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="emotional intelligence social skills text messaging face-to-face communication longitudinal study" search_time="2026年5月21日12时29分星期四"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:34"><title>Neuroscience Research: Support for Social-Emotional and Cognitive Learning</title><summary>Recent findings of neuroscientists offer educators insights into what kinds of instructional formats and strategies are likely to help students develop social, emotional, and cognitive competencies for success.</summary><hostname>Taylor & Francis Online</hostname><publisher>Kappa Delta Pi Record</publisher><author_list><author name="David A Sousa" /></author_list><url>https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00228958.2021.1851580</url><publish_time>2021年1月12日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:35"><title>Impacts of digital connectivity on Thailand’s Generation Z undergraduates’ social skills and emotional intelligence</title><summary>Notwithstanding the pervasive utilization of digital technology in social and educational realms, an in-depth understanding and exploration of the interrelationships amongst digital connectivity, social skills, and emotional intelligence, particularly within Generation Z demographic-known for their heavy reliance on digital platforms-remains elusive. This study endeavors to address this gap. Applying structural equation modeling, it examined the interrelationships between digital connectivity, social skills, and emotional intelligence, surveying a sample of 518 Generation Z students (comprising 77.61% females, 20.64% males, and 1.74% non-binary) across various academic years and disciplines at a university located in Southern Thailand. PLS-SEM software was employed to evaluate the structural model and substantiate the research hypotheses. Our findings suggest that digital connectivity did not detrimentally impact social skills. However, it negatively influenced emotional intelligence among Generation Z students, observable both at the operational level and in terms of fostering the capacity to regulate one’s own and others’ emotional states. Despite this, social skills proved to significantly enhance emotional intelligence. The same consistent pattern of a positive and significant influence is observed when testing the indirect effect of digital connectivity on emotional intelligence through social skills. Furthermore, it was found that robust and effective digital connectivity could potentially bolster understanding and management of emotions in the digital age, much like well-developed social skills. Hence, this study provides substantial insights into the nuanced impacts of digital connectivity on the social and emotional development of Generation Z students.</summary><hostname>U.S. Department of Education</hostname><publisher>Contemporary Educational Technology</publisher><author_list><author name="Narinthon Imjai" affiliation="Faculty of Management Science, Nakhon Si Thammarat Rajabhat University, Nakhon Si Thammarat, THAILAND" /><author name="Somnuk Aujirapongpan" affiliation="School of Accountancy and Finance, Walailak University, Nakhon Si Thammarat, THAILAND" /><author name="Jaturon Jutidharabongse" affiliation="Faculty of Management Science, Nakhon Si Thammarat Rajabhat University, Nakhon Si Thammarat, THAILAND" /><author name="Berto Usman" affiliation="Faculty of Economics and Business, University of Bengkulu, Bengkulu, INDONESIA" /></author_list><url>https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1417314.pdf</url><publish_time>2023年11月30日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:36"><title>Teachers' Attitudes and Beliefs about Adolescents' Use of Digital Technology and the Effect on Copresence Face-To-Face Social Skills: An Exploratory Study Using Q-Methodology</title><hostname>CORE</hostname><publisher>Digital Commons @ LIU</publisher><author_list><author name="Guillermina Garcia" affiliation="Long Island University LIU Post Campus" /></author_list><url>https://core.ac.uk/download/289249147.pdf</url><publish_time>2018年10月1日0时0分</publish_ti
